1: Industry Bridge Coding and PUMS File Creation Process: PUMS 2020-2024
4: Census Bureau industry codes are a condensed list of codes based on the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS). The NAICS is updated periodically to reflect changes in process of production of goods and services,
5: changes in terminology, growth and decline of industries, and the refinement of category composition. In 2022, the NAICS was updated and census industry codes transitioned to the 2022 NAICS.
6: For the 2022 Census Industry Code List, a total of 38 codes were deleted and 33 codes added. In addition to code changes, there were also 89 industry description changes and updates.
7: Also, 15 NAICS codes were updated with no accompanying change in census code.
9: The public use microdata files (PUMS) publish data for all individual industry codes that meet disclosure requirements and have a minimum of 10,000 weighted cases nationwide.
10: For industry, no detailed industries had to be aggregated. As a result, the 2022 Census Industry Code List and the 2022 ACS PUMS Industry Code List are identical.
13: All of the 2022 industry changes were crosswalked by the Census Bureau to create single vintage variables for industry (INDP, NAICSP).
14: The direct matches and conversion rates are being supplied for informational purposes, note that these have already been applied on the 2020-2024 PUMS file.
17: A direct match occurs when an old code moves in its entirety to a new code between the two most recent classification systems. All data with a particular code from the previous industry
18: code list should be recoded with the new code.
21: Industry data from the American Community Survey (ACS) between 2019 and 2022 were double coded with the new and the old classification systems.
22: For each old industry that was bridgecoded, coders were provided with a list of possible new industry that these cases could be recoded to.
23: Each 2019-2022 code could only be given one of a restricted set of codes. After bridge coding, each bridge-coded case had a record with the previously assigned industry codes
24: along with the new industry codes. This double-coding allowed for the creation of conversion rates, which can be used to bridge classification systems.
27: Conversion rates are calculated for industry codes that split into two or more new codes.
28: For all cases that were bridgecoded, we determined the weighted proportion of cases that split into new industry codes for each old industry code.
30: Two different sets of conversion rates were created: a total conversion rate and a more refined conversion rate that incorporated sex and educational attainment. After examining preliminary files,
31: the Census Bureau determined that a total conversion rate was not sufficiently refined and created a new set of conversion rates incorporating sex and educational attainment (3 levels of educational attainment).
32: The refined conversion rates more accurately captured the demographic variation. Though we recommend using the sex by educational attainment conversion rate where feasible, both versions are provided to the public.

43: There were some combinations of industry, sex, and educational attainment that were not observed in the data. Because these combinations are theoretically possible,
44: we set those conversion rates to 0.0001 to allow for the possibility of someone being assigned that combination of characteristics.
47: The PUMS conversion rates should be used when comparing data from published tables created with ACS PUMS data or when analyzing the PUMS microdata files. Microdata files provide records for every respondent in
48: the sample. The conversion rates need to be applied to each record with a code that needs bridgecoded. The recommended method for applying the conversion rates is through a 4-step process.
50: First, create cut-off intervals from the table of conversion rates.  To create the cut-offs, start at 0, then cumulatively add the conversion rates within a code on the older classification; the last interval should always end
51: with 1. These cut-offs create intervals with sizes, or proportions, reflecting the conversion rates.  That is, the intervals are mutually exclusive and cover the proportion of the numbers between 0 and 1 with the same
52: proportions as the conversion rates. Table 1 provides an example for the 2017 PUMS industry code 6672 - Internet publishing and broadcasting and web search portals. In the example, the areas for the four intervals
53: are, respectively, 0.0073, 0.0174, 0.7133, and 0.2620, thus reflecting the conversion rates for that code. Also, the intervals are mutually exclusive and together cover all possible random numbers between 0 and 1.
54: Note that the conversion rates shown are rounded, so the proportions derived from the cut-offs may not exactly match the proportions shown in the conversion rates.
56: Table 1. Example of Cut-off Intervals for Applying Conversion Rates to Microdata.
63: Second, generate a random number for each record using a uniform distribution between 0 and 1. This means that all such numbers generated will be evenly distributed between 0 and 1.
64: Third, compare a record’s random number, x, to the appropriate conversion rate cut-offs. Fourth, the new classification code should be selected if x falls between the corresponding cut-offs.
66: Table 2 provides an example using a subset of imitation ACS PUMS microdata for four records with 2017 industry code 6672. For every record, assign a random number using a random number generator.
67: Then, compare the random number to the cut-off intervals from Table 1. Finally, assign the 2022 code that corresponds to each interval.
69: Table 2. Example of Imitation PUMS Microdata Subset by 2017 Industry Code 6672.
77: Also, the user may want to maintain per-record consistency in the generated random number across different instances of data processing. To do this, the user should specify a seed, per data year, and specify a record sort order.
78: Note also that even slightly different versions of a statistical program, e.g., SAS, may have different random number generators with different underlying algorithms.
